386.title: Lead me on
386.hook: the Handbook ends with old lines: Cleanthes asking to be led willingly, Socrates saying they can kill but not harm him (Enchiridion 52–53)
386.howItsDone: Some people practicing Stoicism memorize a few short lines, such as the closing sayings of the Enchiridion, and repeat them in hard moments.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was agōn, the contest that can't be put off. Your line was the contest is now.

Most books end with a summary. The handbook ends with a pocketful of old lines: not Epictetus' own words, but sayings from a poet, a hymn writer and Socrates, the way some people keep a folded note in a wallet. Before he hands them over, there's one last short lesson about why people know so much and do so little. Then four sayings, to be kept at hand, he says, always. The handbook was made to be carried. These are what he wanted carried last.
screen: `THE HANDBOOK ENDS WITH OLD LINES.` → `A FOLDED NOTE IN A WALLET.` → `LEAD ME ON.`

segments.voice: Section fifty-two says philosophy has three parts. The first and most necessary is using the principles: for example, don't lie. The second is the proof: why one shouldn't lie. The third checks the proofs: what makes a proof, what's true, what's false. The third exists for the second, and the second for the first. But people do the reverse, he says. They spend their time on the third, and so they lie, while perfectly ready to prove that lying is wrong. Then the last section. The first saying is by Cleanthes, the school's second head: Lead me, Zeus, and you, Destiny, wherever you've set me. I'll follow without hesitating. And if I'm unwilling, and turn bad, I'll follow all the same. Seneca put these lines into Latin, and his version ends: the fates lead the willing, and drag the unwilling. From the poet Euripides: whoever yields well to necessity is wise among us, and knows the things of the gods. From Socrates, in prison, to his friend Crito: if this pleases the gods, so be it. And the book's last line, Socrates again, at his trial: Anytus and Meletus, his accusers, can kill me, but they cannot harm me. The handbook stops there. Not with an argument, but with a man who knew which part of him was out of anyone's reach. Whether or not you share their picture of Zeus and destiny, the question stays: when the road goes where you didn't choose, will you walk it, or be dragged?

segments.voice: Let one of the four sayings stay with you: lead me on; yield well to what must be; if it pleases the gods, so be it; they can kill me, but not harm me. Or, if none of these is yours, another old line that has steadied you, from scripture, a poem, or a person you loved. Say it quietly, once, then again, slower, and let it settle like a stone in a pocket.

Your line: willingly. The road is the same either way; the walking is yours. Onward, day three hundred eighty-six.

387.title: Handbook close
387.hook: fifty-three chapters in fifty-six days; the handbook is now yours to carry
387.howItsDone: Many people who study the Enchiridion keep a few favorite sections written on a card or in a notebook and return to them daily, as Arrian intended the book to be kept at hand.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Cleanthes, whose hymn opens the handbook's last section. Your line was willingly.

Fifty-three short sections in fifty-six days. That's the handbook, read in order, start to finish. Eight weeks ago it opened with Arrian, the student who boiled his teacher's lessons down into a little book meant to be kept in the hand. The Greek name, enchiridion, means just that: the thing in the hand, a word also used for a small knife. Today it closes. Not to go on a shelf. A handbook on a shelf has missed its whole point.
screen: `FIFTY-THREE SECTIONS, FIFTY-SIX DAYS.` → `THE THING IN THE HAND.` → `HANDBOOK CLOSE.`

segments.voice: Section one split the world into two piles: what is up to us, our judgments, desires and choices, and what isn't, our body, property, reputation and office. The line was start here, and almost everything after flowed from that one sort. Section five gave its sharpest form: people are disturbed not by things, but by their judgments about things. Then the everyday tools. The jug you love is a jug. The baths will have splashing and shoving, so keep your purpose. When the dish comes around, take a modest share. You're an actor in a play; play your part well. The insult only harms through your judgment. Count the cost first. Then living with other people. What the role asks. Mostly quiet. Yes means yes. Ask, don't tell. He missed the rest. The table matters. It seemed right to him. Two handles. Quickly, not badly. These can be the hardest to keep, because they happen in conversation, fast, with no time to look anything up. And the road: signs of progress, starting with blame no one. Live the book, not just explain it. How long will you wait? And at the very end, Cleanthes: lead me on, and I'll follow willingly. Arrian made this book to be carried, and no one carries fifty-three things. So the last practice is a choice: three lines to keep in the hand. Tomorrow a new part of the path begins: the Discourses, the longer record of Epictetus actually teaching, joking and scolding in his classroom.

388.title: The classroom at Nicopolis
388.hook: the Discourses are a student's notes of Epictetus teaching young men
388.howItsDone: Some readers of the Discourses read passages aloud, since Arrian says he tried to keep his teacher's spoken words rather than write a polished book.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was enchiridion, the thing in the hand: a handbook closed, and three lines kept. Your line was carry three.

Northwest Greece, under the Roman emperors. A city by the sea with a name that means victory city. In a room somewhere in it, a teacher who was once enslaved is talking to a class of young men. He teases them. He loses patience with them. He tells them stories about their own vanity until they squirm. And in the room, a student is writing down every word he can catch. A new part of the path begins here.
screen: `A CITY CALLED VICTORY.` → `A TEACHER, ONCE ENSLAVED.` → `THE CLASSROOM AT NICOPOLIS.`

segments.voice: Epictetus was enslaved in Rome. Ancient writers name his owner: Epaphroditus, himself a freedman who had served Nero. Epictetus studied philosophy with the Stoic Musonius Rufus, and at some point was freed. Then, the writer Aulus Gellius reports, the emperor Domitian expelled the philosophers from Rome, and Epictetus moved across the sea to Nicopolis. In victory city he opened a school, and young men came to hear him. One of those students was Arrian, who later wrote a history of Alexander the Great. Arrian wrote down what he heard. In a short letter at the front of the Discourses, he says he didn't compose them like a book. He tried to record his teacher's words as nearly as he could, in the very words used, as reminders of his thinking and his frankness. That's why they sound like speech, full of questions and jokes and rough corners. The handbook was the summary. The Discourses are the classroom. You'll hear Epictetus interrupt, argue with imaginary students, mock the proud and lose patience with the lazy. It's the difference between reading a recipe and standing in the kitchen. For the next weeks, this path stands in the kitchen.

389.title: The gift of use
389.hook: the gods gave us one thing wholly ours: the right use of impressions (Discourses 1.1)
389.howItsDone: People practicing Stoicism often pause on a strong first impression, such as an insult or a fear, and examine whether it is true before acting on it, which Epictetus calls the right use of impressions.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Arrian, the student who wrote down his teacher's very words. Your line was a real classroom.

Spell-check can tell you a word is misspelled. It can't tell you whether to send the email. A music app can tell you the song is in the right key. It can't tell you whether this is the moment to sing it. Each tool judges its own work and goes quiet on whether to use it. The very first discourse in the book opens with the same observation, using the tools of Epictetus' day. Then it asks: so what in us can answer the real question?
screen: `SPELL-CHECK CAN'T TELL YOU TO SEND IT.` → `EVERY TOOL IS SILENT ABOUT SOMETHING.` → `THE GIFT OF USE.`

segments.voice: Look at all the skills and faculties, Epictetus says, and you won't find one that examines itself. Grammar can judge what's written, but if you're writing to a friend, grammar won't tell you whether to write. Music can judge a tune, but not whether to sing or play right now. What will tell you? The faculty that examines itself and everything else: reason. Only it asks what it is, what it can do, and what it's worth. Gold doesn't tell you gold is beautiful. Something in you does, by how it uses the impression of gold. So the gods, Epictetus says, put in our power only the best thing, the ruler of all the rest: the right use of impressions. Everything else they left outside our power. Then he imagines Zeus explaining himself. If I could have, Zeus says, I would have made your body and your little property free too. But your body isn't really yours. It's clay, cleverly mixed. Since I couldn't, I gave you a part of myself: this power to choose and refuse, to desire and avoid, to use impressions. Look after it, and you'll never be blocked. You might believe in Zeus, in God, in nature, in evolution, or in none of these, and the point still lands. You didn't get to choose most of what happens. You did get one thing that's wholly yours: what you do with how things appear to you. An impression arrives: they're ignoring me. You get to examine it before you agree. That's the gift, and it's yours by use, not by owning it.

390.title: Not even Zeus
390.hook: "I'll chain your leg." "My leg, yes; my will, not even Zeus can conquer" (Discourses 1.1)
390.howItsDone: People practicing Stoicism often rehearse hard situations in advance and ask, inside each constraint, what still belongs to them: their choices, judgments and attention.

segments.voice: Yesterday: grammar, gold, and Zeus explaining his one gift, the right use of impressions. Your line was the gift of use.

A tyrant leans across the table and lists what he can do to you. Chains. Prison. Worse. Epictetus stages this scene in the first discourse as a quick back-and-forth, almost like a comedy sketch. He wasn't writing from the safe side of power. He grew up enslaved, with no say over his own body, and that gives his answers a particular weight. Notice who gets the funny lines. It isn't the man with the chains.
screen: `A TYRANT LISTS WHAT HE CAN DO.` → `CHAINS. PRISON. WORSE.` → `NOT EVEN ZEUS.`

segments.voice: Later in the first discourse, Epictetus runs through the hard things. I must die. Must I die groaning too? I must be chained. Must I also whine about it? I must be exiled. Does anyone stop me from going with a smile, cheerful and calm? Then the scene. Tell me your secrets, says the tyrant. I won't; that's up to me. Then I'll chain you. What are you saying, man? You'll chain my leg. My will, not even Zeus can overpower. I'll throw you in prison. You mean my little body. I'll cut off your head. Well, when did I ever tell you mine was the only neck in the world that couldn't be cut? The will he means is prohairesis, the power to choose, to judge, to assent or refuse. In the Discourses it names the part of you that's truly yours. A tyrant can move your body anywhere. He can't make you agree that his threat is your harm. Later writers told a story that Epictetus' master once twisted his leg, and Epictetus calmly warned, you'll break it. When it broke, he said: didn't I tell you? Nobody knows if that happened, and another ancient source says he was simply lame from illness. But the Discourses never ask anyone to pretend chains don't hurt. They ask a narrower question: inside this constraint, what is still yours? These, Epictetus says, are the things to rehearse, to write down every day, to practice. Not because a tyrant is coming. Because small chains come every week.
screen: `MUST I DIE GROANING TOO?` · `MY LEG, YES. MY WILL, NOT EVEN ZEUS.` · `PROHAIRESIS: THE POWER TO CHOOSE.` · `INSIDE THE CONSTRAINT, WHAT'S YOURS?` · then, large: `NOT EVEN ZEUS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one constraint you're living inside right now, a job you can't leave yet, an illness, a tight budget, a body that won't do what it used to, and name it plainly. 391.title: Knowing your price
391.hook: Agrippinus kept his character though it cost him; each person knows their own price (Discourses 1.2)
391.howItsDone: People practicing Stoicism sometimes decide in advance on a few things they will not do for any reward, so that when the offer comes they don't have to deliberate.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was prohairesis, the will that not even Zeus can overpower. Your line was what is still yours.

Agrippinus is being tried before the Senate in Rome. A messenger runs to tell him. Agrippinus says: good luck to it. But it's the hour for exercise and a cold bath. Let's go. Later the messenger comes back. You've been condemned. To exile, or to death? Exile. And my property? Not taken. Then let's go out to Aricia and have lunch. Epictetus tells that one in the first discourse. In the second, he tells another story about him, about a question Agrippinus refused even to think about.
screen: `AGRIPPINUS, ON TRIAL.` → `EXILE? THEN LET'S HAVE LUNCH.` → `KNOWING YOUR PRICE.`

segments.voice: The second discourse is titled, roughly, how to keep your own character in everything. The Greek word for character there is prosōpon, the mask and role from the handbook. Epictetus imagines someone asking whether to hold the chamber pot for another man. If he refuses, he'll be beaten and go without food. For a different person, it would be unbearable not only to hold it, but even to let someone else hold it for him. If you ask me, Epictetus says, I'll tell you food is worth more than hunger and a beating is worse than none, so if that's how you measure, go and hold it. But it's beneath me? That, he says, is something you bring to the question, not me. You know what you're worth to yourself, and at what price you sell yourself. People sell themselves at different prices. Then Agrippinus. A man named Florus was weighing whether to take part in one of Nero's spectacles, appearing on stage to please the emperor. He asked Agrippinus, who said: go. Then why won't you? Because, said Agrippinus, I don't even consider the question. Once you start weighing such things, Epictetus says, setting the value of outside things against each other, you're close to those who've forgotten their own character. Agrippinus didn't win the argument about Nero's stage. He never let it become an argument. Knowing your price isn't pride. It's knowing, before the offer arrives, the few things that simply aren't for sale.

segments.voice: Ask yourself quietly what you wouldn't do, even if it paid well, even if everyone else was doing it: laughing at a cruel joke to fit in, shading the truth for a sale, flattering someone to get ahead. Find one, and picture the moment it's offered. Then picture yourself not even weighing it, just a plain no.
Agrippinus. The man who wouldn't even consider some questions; you know at what price you sell yourself. Today's word.
Your line: I know my price. Some questions never need weighing at all, not even once. Until tomorrow.

392.title: The purple thread
392.hook: Epictetus wants to be the purple stripe in the robe, the small part that makes the rest beautiful (Discourses 1.2)
392.howItsDone: Readers of the Stoics often keep the image of the purple stripe as a reminder that one person's conduct can set the tone for a room, a family or a workplace.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Agrippinus, who wouldn't even consider some questions. Your line was I know my price.

A Roman senator's tunic was mostly plain wool, with broad bands of purple running down it. That purple came from sea snails, crushed by the thousands, and it cost a fortune. A narrow strip of color on a big garment, and the part everyone saw. Epictetus told his students he wanted to be the purple in the garment. Not the whole cloak. Not even most of it. Just the thin bright strip that makes the rest look good.
screen: `PLAIN WOOL, BANDS OF PURPLE.` → `DYE FROM SEA SNAILS.` → `I WANT TO BE THAT STRIPE.`

segments.voice: It comes in the same chapter as yesterday, Discourses book one, chapter two, wrapped around a story about a senator named Helvidius Priscus. The emperor Vespasian sent word: don't come to the senate. Helvidius answered, more or less: you can remove me, but while I'm a senator, I go. Then go, and keep quiet. Don't ask my opinion, and I'll keep quiet. But I have to ask it. Then I have to say what seems right. Then I'll have you killed. And Helvidius said: did I ever tell you I couldn't die? You do your part, and I'll do mine. Then the practical question: what good did one man do? What good does the purple do the cloak? It doesn't keep anyone warmer. It stands out, and it sets an example for the rest. He'd used the image a few lines earlier. Someone tells him: be like everyone else, just one thread among the many. Fine, Epictetus says, for someone who sees himself that way. But I want to be the purple. He isn't saying everyone has to be heroic, or that the plain wool is worthless. A cloak is mostly wool. He's saying each person decides what kind of thread to be, and that one bright strand changes how the whole garment looks. The week in one breath: willingly, carry three, a real classroom, the gift of use, not even Zeus, I know my price, and now the purple thread.
screen: `HELVIDIUS AND THE EMPEROR.` · `WHAT GOOD DID ONE MAN DO?` · `THE STRIPE SHOWS WHAT A CLOAK CAN BE.` · `YOU CHOOSE WHICH THREAD TO BE.` · then, large: `THE PURPLE THREAD.`

segments.voice: Picture one ordinary moment coming up, a meeting, a family dinner, a line at the store, as a plain cloak with everyone going along. Then look for where a thin bright thread could run through it: the honest answer, the kind word, the person who stays calm. You don't have to change the whole room, only see the one strand you could be.
Helvidius Priscus. The senator who defied an emperor and kept his own character; the small part that shows the rest what it could be.
Your line: the bright strand. A cloak is mostly wool, and that's all right. Day three hundred ninety-two, and a week done.
